1:
Clarke and Calvin disagree flatly about what the psalmist escaped. Clarke, having noted "a strange and numerous diversity of opinions", settles on the same occasion as the two preceding psalms: "a thanksgiving for his recovery from the sore disease by which he was afflicted in his body". Calvin rejects exactly that: "some are of opinion, but without good reason, that it ought to be understood of sickness. It is rather to be supposed that David here comprehends a multitude of dangers." Delitzsch takes the author to be David "though not without some hesitation", and places him between two states: "just been rescued from danger, and, on the other, is still exposed to peril."

Clarke also makes a structural claim nobody else raises: "from the eleventh to the end contains a new subject and appears to have belonged to another Psalm."

Who is speaking divides them from the first line. Gill hears Christ throughout, the patience exercised "in the garden, when he submitted himself entirely to the will of God; and on the cross". Spurgeon agrees: "Job on the dunghill does not equal Jesus on the cross." Henry takes it of David's own inward trouble and then applies it. Wesley marks a seam instead: the fifth verse "seems to be interposed as a wall of partition, between that which David speaks in his own person, and that which he speaks in the person of the Messiah".

The doubled verb is heard by grammarians and preachers alike. Ellicott identifies the idiom and renders it "I waited and waited"; Calvin draws the length out of the repetition, then turns it into doctrine: "although God may not forthwith appear for our help, but rather of design keep us in suspense, yet we must not lose courage." Henry states the rule more briefly: "those whose expectation is from God may wait with assurance, but must wait with patience."

Augustine argues from the creditworthiness of the promiser. He waited "for the promise of no mere mortal who can both deceive and be himself deceived"; God "though He puts off the fulfilment of His promises, yet never recalls them", being "a sponsible Promiser; a faithful Paymaster" — so the weak should claim mercy as lambs do, "striking their dams' teats with their heads."

The pit is where the philology bites. Clarke takes it literally: "the sounding pit; where nothing was heard except the howlings of wild beasts, or the hollow sounds of winds". Ellicott allows the same primary sense — "the idea of a noise of rushing water suits this passage" — but reports that most take the word for "destruction". He then argues the scene into metaphor: the rock is "the common image of security, the occurrence of which makes it probable that the pit and clay are also not realities, but emblems of confusion and danger." Henry reaches that conclusion by another road, the psalm mentioning neither sickness nor enemies here: "despondency of spirit under the sense of God's withdrawings, and prevailing doubts and fears about the eternal state, are indeed a horrible pit and miry clay." Wesley keeps it general — "desperate dangers and calamities".

What makes the song new is disputed. Clarke makes it new to the singer, since "cheerfulness and joy had long been strangers to him"; Ellicott looks for the novelty in the content, its newness lying "in the magnificent vindication of spiritual above formal worship"; Gill identifies the song with the fifth verse and gives it to the risen Christ.

The blessed man is defined by what he refuses. Ellicott renders it "turneth not towards proud men and false apostates", admitting the words are "somewhat obscure"; where others read "turners after idols", "idolatry is doubtless implied, but not expressed." Wesley identifies the lies as worldly power, wisdom and riches, "called lies, because they promise more than they perform".
6:
These three verses are where the Hebrew and the Greek part company: the Hebrew says the ears were opened, the Greek, followed by the Epistle to the Hebrews, that a body was prepared. Clarke states the problem without softening it: David's words "might be more properly rendered, My ears hast thou bored", meaning "Thou hast made me thy servant for ever", after the law by which a slave refusing freedom had his ear pierced. "But how is it possible," he asks, "that the Septuagint and the apostle should take a meaning so totally different from the sense of the Hebrew?" His answer is a conjecture he reports approvingly: that the Hebrew is corrupt, the word for ears standing where the original read "Then, a Body", the two being easy to confuse.

Ellicott takes the received Hebrew and rules out both other readings by one observation. The literal sense is "Ears hast thou dug for me, which can hardly mean anything but Thou hast given me the sense of hearing", so that "the attentive ear and obedient heart, not formal rites, constitute true worship". Then the argument: the noun is plural, and that plural "sets aside the idea of a revelation", elsewhere expressed by opening a single ear, and "excludes allusion to the symbolic act by which a slave was devoted to perpetual servitude, because then also only one ear was bored." He is no more impressed by a modern emendation giving "Shouldest thou desire sacrifice and offering I would select the fattest" — "a most desirable result if his arguments were accepted."

The rest keep the bored ear. Wesley glosses it "Heb. bored — I have devoted myself to thy perpetual service", noting that "the seventy Jewish interpreters, whom the apostle follows, translate these words, a body hast thou prepared me." Spurgeon refuses to drop either sense: the ears "were as if excavated down to his soul", and yet "there is no reason to reject the notion that the digging of the ear may refer to the boring of the ear of the servant."

What the rejected sacrifices lacked is set out most fully by Henry: they could not "take away the terror of sin by pacifying the conscience, nor the power of sin by sanctifying the nature", their value resting on "their reference to Jesus Christ, of whom they were types — shadows of good things to come". Spurgeon puts the obsolescence in an image: the offerings "had their worth, but when Jesus, the Antitype, came into the world, they ceased to be of value, as candles are of no estimation when the sun has arisen." Delitzsch reads it as a structured negative answer to the question how thanks are to be rendered; Gill and Wesley guard the claim, since the sacrifices were once acceptable.

The book of the seventh verse divides the antiquarian from the grammarian. Clarke identifies it: the book "must be the Pentateuch; for, in David's time no other part of Divine revelation had been committed to writing." Ellicott rejects the whole construction: the received rendering, "which follows the LXX. and Vulg., and is adopted in the Epistle to the Hebrews, must be abandoned." The Hebrew means "Lo! I come, bringing the book written for me" — the Law produced as warrant for conduct performed; the alternative, "written on me", "might suit the contents of the book, but not the roll itself."

Delight in the will is where the argument turns. Wesley calls it "an act of heroic obedience, that he not only resolved to do, but delighted in doing the will of God" — a will that was "to die, and that a most shameful, and painful, and cursed death". Clarke draws the consequence: since the essence of the old system lay in its sacrifices and God will not have them, "the introduction of the Messiah into the world is the abolition of the law."
9:
The verb rendered "preached" is not really preaching, and two of them say so from different angles. Ellicott gives the literal sense — "I have made countenances glad" — and notices the form, "the rapid succession of clauses, like successive wave-beats of praise." Delitzsch supplies the etymology: the root means to rub smooth, hence "to make him joyful and glad, more especially to cheer one by good news", the word being "in Hebrew directly equivalent to" the Greek for evangelising.

Who the great congregation is divides them. Clarke is definite: it "means the Gentiles, contradistinguished from the Jews." Gill takes it of the Jewish festivals, when all the males were obliged to appear; Wesley keeps both, "not only to the Jews, but also to all nations". What was preached divides them further: for Clarke the righteousness is "God's method of justifying sinners by faith, without the deeds of the law", for Gill "the righteousness which Christ himself wrought out", for Wesley simply "thy faithfulness".

The turn from praise to petition is noticed by two voices independently, in the same terms. Delitzsch calls it method — "in accordance with the true art of prayer, petition developes itself out of thanksgiving" — and points out that the two withholdings answer each other: "he refrained not his lips; therefore, on His part, let not Jahve withhold His tender mercies." Spurgeon: "he had not withheld his testimony to God's truth, now in return he begs his Father not to withhold his compassion."

Clarke weighs the petition's words separately: the tender mercies are "such propensities and feelings as a mother bears to her child", the truth "what is revealed in thy word" — so that it is "mercy to help me, truth to direct me."

Who is speaking here is the tile's real question, and the answers split three ways. Henry marks a change of person: having spoken "in the person of the Messiah", the psalmist "now comes to make improvement of the doctrine of his mediation... and therefore speaks in his own person" — and makes the petition an argument from the greater to the less: "thou hast not spared thy Son, nor withheld him; withhold not thou thy tender mercies then." Wesley reads the same return, David being "led back by the same spirit, to the consideration of his own case". Spurgeon keeps Christ as the speaker throughout, the mercies being "for awhile withheld from our Lord while on the accursed tree", and "the coming of the angel to strengthen him was a clear answer to his prayer"; he allows too that the verse "might more correctly be read as a declaration of his confidence that help would not be refused".

The confession of iniquity is where that question becomes acute. Gill and Spurgeon keep it in Christ's mouth by making the sins another's: the evils are "the evils of punishment inflicted on him, as the surety and Saviour of his people", and "our sins were innumerable, and so were his griefs." Clarke refuses the placement instead: "this part does not comport with the preceding; and either argues a former experience, or must be considered a part of another Psalm." His reason is psychological rather than doctrinal — the words "could not be said by any person who was exulting in the pardoning mercy of God, as David was at the time he penned the commencement of this Psalm."

Read of David, the verse yields one image that two of them reach for. Henry sees the sins "taking hold of him, arresting him, as the bailiff does the poor debtor", the man finding that "in all the reviews of his life... still he discovered something amiss"; Wesley uses the same figure. Delitzsch keeps the door open both ways, treating the evils as those "which come even upon the righteous as trials or as chastenings".
13:
Two voices note independently that the psalm ends by becoming another psalm. Ellicott states it as a fact of the text: "from this verse onwards, with some trifling variations", the passage recurs elsewhere in the Psalter as a separate composition. Clarke had already argued the same thing on internal grounds, and the two together make the closing section look less like a conclusion than like a second poem attached to the first.

Delitzsch reads the petition as the natural issue of the confession before it: "in the midst of such sufferings, which, the longer they last, discover him all the more to himself as a sinner, he prays for speedy help." He notes where the cry is aimed — the verb "turns... towards the will of God; for this is the root of all things" — and describes the wish against the enemies as a recoil rather than a curse, "that the purpose of his deadly foes may as it were rebound against the protection of God and miserably miscarry."

Gill takes every clause of the imprecation as fulfilled history read forward. The deliverance prayed for was granted "when he was raised from the dead"; the shame belongs to "the last day, when they shall see him whom they have pierced come in the clouds of heaven"; the desolation was executed in fact, since "their habitations in Jerusalem were desolate, and so was their house or temple there, and their whole land". Wesley reduces the same verse to its motive, the shame being the enemies' own "sinful and shameful actions".

The prayer for others is read as a request for constancy rather than for relief. Delitzsch has David wishing that the pious "may most heartily rejoice in God, the goal of their longing", and that on account of the salvation they love "they may continually say: Let Jahve become great." Clarke makes the same continually a matter of supply: "in making prayer and supplication to thee, let them ever find thee, that they may magnify thee for the blessings they receive." He also narrows who is meant by those that love the salvation — not all who wish to be spared, but those "who earnestly desire to be saved from sin: saved in thy own way, and on thy own terms."

The last verse is where Clarke's word-by-word method pays. The two adjectives are not synonyms: the first means "afflicted, greatly depressed", the second "a beggar. One utterly destitute, and seeking help." And the divine name is a claim rather than an address — "my prop, my support" — while the verb of thinking is stronger than it looks, since the Lord "meditateth, upon me". Out of that he draws the whole argument of the psalm in one sentence: "seeing that my miserable state occupies thy heart, it will soon employ thy hand. Thou, who meditatest upon me, wilt deliver me."

Delitzsch marks the same movement structurally: with the emphatic pronoun the psalmist "comes back to his own present helpless state, but only in order to contrast with it the confession of confident hope." Poor and needy he is, "but He who ruleth over all will care for him." Gill keeps the sufferer identified with Christ to the end, poor "literally" and poor in a spiritual sense when "deserted by his Father, forsaken by his disciples, and surrounded by his enemies".

Clarke closes on the haste. Since God is "disposed to help, and I am in such great necessity, delay not, but come speedily to my assistance" — and he leaves the last word to an old psalter, which turns the request from rescue into perseverance: "let us not be so long under distress and misery that we lose our patience, or our love to thee."
